title: The Recipe Card
passage_text:
The recipe card was stained with vanilla and folded at one corner, and when Jasmine found it tucked inside her grandmother's cookbook, she almost threw it away with the rest of the clutter from the kitchen drawer.

Instead, she read the faded handwriting, and suddenly she was seven years old again, standing on a wooden stool in the same kitchen while her grandmother guided her small hands to crack eggs into a yellow bowl. "Slow and steady," Grandma Lou had said, laughing as a piece of shell slipped into the batter. "Every good cake starts with a little mess." Jasmine had not thought about that afternoon in years, but she could still hear the radio playing old gospel songs while the oven warmed the room.

Now Jasmine was fifteen, and the house felt too quiet since Grandma Lou had moved into the assisted living center across town. Her parents were packing boxes for the estate sale on Saturday, and everyone kept saying it was time to let go of old things.

She slipped the card into her jacket pocket without telling anyone. Later, she would realize that this small decision would change the way her whole family spent the following weekend.

That evening, Jasmine gathered flour, sugar, butter, and eggs, and she followed the instructions one careful step at a time. The batter looked lumpy, and she was sure she had measured the baking powder wrong, but she kept going, remembering her grandmother's patient voice.

On Sunday afternoon, Jasmine carried the cake, still slightly lopsided, into the bright dining room at the center. Grandma Lou looked at it for a long moment, then reached for her granddaughter's hand. "You remembered," she whispered, and for the first time in months, the whole family sat around one table, sharing slices and stories until visiting hours ended.
